item.title: @StockSavvyShay：投资人回顾2026年市场波动与成长股回调，分享晋升父亲的个人感悟
item.description:
I have a lot to be thankful for this year but I don't think I've ever approached Thanksgiving with a greater appreciation for what actually matters because 2026 has tested me in just so many ways while also giving me something I've dreamed about for most of my life.

This year reminded me that building something you genuinely love doesn't mean every part of journey is going to be enjoyable especially when you're sharing your investments/ideas with thousands of people through one of most difficult drawdowns growth investors have experienced in years and it's one thing to share your ideas when everything is working but it's an entirely different experience when markets turn against you and people are looking to you for perspective while you're navigating those same challenges yourself but somewhere in middle of all that my biggest dream came true and I became a father.

6 months ago my wife and I welcomed our son into the world and between becoming parents and moving into our home earlier this year my life looks completely different from where it was last Thanksgiving... where we now have this little boy who has absolutely no idea what Nasdaq is doing or where VIX is trading or how much money mr market decided to erase on any particular afternoon.

And there have been just so many days this year where I've spent hours staring at screens trying to make sense of another painful move in growth stocks only to walk away from my desk and see my son smiling at me like there's not a single thing wrong in the world and it's amazing how quickly everything else becomes less important in those moments.

I really have spent so much of my adult life focused on building a career/creating opportunities for future but becoming a father has made me realize that the life I've been working so hard to build is already happening right in front of me even on days when market makes it difficult to appreciate much else and it's a perspective I don't think I could have fully understood until becoming a parent and I think that's what makes this Thanksgiving feel so different from the last one.

And if there's one thing 2026 has taught me is that you can have one of hardest years of your professional life and still be living through the greatest year of your personal life.

Happy Thanksgiving to you and your families and I genuinely appreciate every single one of you.

I like this combination because cheaper compute drives way more inference demand as adoption really just began a couple months ago while roughly a third of planned AI capacity could still be waiting for electricity by 2028 so even if the AI buildout slows from 60 mph to 45 mph there's still a stupid amount of power infrastructure that needs to be built.

And I actually think space might be where I get most aggressive heading into year end because I see this as a decade long infrastructure opportunity driven by falling launch costs, satellite connectivity and growing defense demand rather than the same AI financing concerns currently weighing on growth stocks.

item.title: @jukan05：韩媒分析称三星与SK海力士长期协议预付款变动显示约束力存疑
item.description:
Samsung Electronics and SK hynix say their long term agreements (LTAs) are now more binding than before, but Korean media reported that the advance payments recorded on their books make that claim hard to support.

According to SK hynix's 2026 third quarter report, contract liabilities, which represent the obligation to deliver products after receiving payment from customers in advance, have barely moved from around KRW 500 billion over the past year. The company explained that because transactions are conducted through various methods such as deposits, it is difficult to judge long term agreements based on contract liabilities or advance payments alone. However, escrow, guarantees, and collateral are arrangements where money can only be recovered through set procedures if a contract is broken. If the company had truly strengthened the binding force of its agreements, there should be some other reason for choosing these methods over receiving advance payments directly. One accountant also noted that escrow is not a common arrangement, pointing out that a company can earn at least interest simply by receiving the money directly and putting it to work, so there is no reason to deposit it with a third party.

Samsung Electronics is in a different situation. Its contract liabilities, which had stayed within a set range for several years, rose by about KRW 8.5 trillion quarter on quarter in the second quarter of this year to KRW 23.6 trillion as it signed long term agreements with large customers. The company said advance payments would grow further as additional contracts were signed. In the third quarter, however, contract liabilities related to advance payments rose by only about KRW 550 billion. The industry believes Samsung may have reduced the amount of upfront payments in the additional contracts in exchange for raising the price cap on semiconductors. If this interpretation is correct, it does not match the company's description of "sufficiently binding LTAs." This is because lower advance payments make it easier for customers to walk away from contracts if the memory supply and demand balance reverses.

被回答的问题 @VanquishTrader
WHY 2027 COULD BE THE YEAR $IREN PROVES EVERYONE WRONG

Market has completely misunderstood IREN and I believe 2027 could be the year investors finally recognize just how dramatically the underlying business has changed.

While shares have experienced an enormous drawdown alongside the broader neocloud sector, the company's financial results tell a very different story, with Q1 revenue increasing 66% sequentially to $228M, AI Cloud revenue nearly tripling to $200M, operating ARR doubling to $1B and contracted backlog expanding to $20.3B, with approximately two-thirds tied to investment-grade customers.

Adjusted EBITDA also increased from $19M to $66M as margins expanded from 14% to 29%, which I find particularly impressive considering IREN is still in the earliest stages of its transformation into an AI infrastructure company.

Yet investors increasingly appear to be interpreting Microsoft's deployment delays and management's decision to moderate capital spending as evidence of deteriorating demand, when I think the bigger issue is that demand for AI computing continues expanding faster than the industry's ability to finance and deploy the infrastructure required to support it.

And that is an important distinction because there is an enormous difference between a company struggling to find customers and one struggling to bring enough capacity online to satisfy the customers it already has.

What makes IREN particularly interesting to me is that the company isn't simply purchasing billions of dollars in GPUs and hoping future rental prices remain attractive, but has spent years building an underlying infrastructure footprint consisting of land, power connections and data centers that becomes increasingly valuable as electricity availability constrains AI development.

With more than 5GW of secured power and approximately $6B in data center assets that management describes as unencumbered, IREN has established a foundation that would take competitors years and substantial capital to replicate, although only around 0.1GW of AI capacity was operational at September's end.

And we're already seeing how valuable usable computing infrastructure has become, with IREN recently signing a five-year agreement generating approximately $22M in annual revenue per megawatt alongside customer prepayments covering 90% of associated GPU capital expenditures, while shorter-duration agreements have reached $40M per megawatt.

Even older H100 GPUs are being recontracted at twice their original pricing, challenging the assumption that AI hardware rapidly loses its commercial value as newer generations arrive.

Management's estimated 18-month GPU payback is particularly encouraging, although that doesn't represent recovery of the full infrastructure investment, but the broader opportunity is that IREN could recover its hardware costs relatively quickly while retaining ownership of data center assets capable of supporting successive generations of computing technology.

Now I completely understand why investors remain skeptical because converting a $20.3B backlog into recognized revenue requires enormous capital investment, and the economics only become attractive if IREN can bring that capacity online without financing costs consuming the returns.

Microsoft's requested network changes at Childress pushed management's more than $4B operating ARR target from December into January or potentially February 2027, with Horizon 1 already operational and the remaining deployments progressing through commissioning and customer acceptance.

I don't believe a relatively short delay fundamentally changes the economics of a multiyear customer agreement, but it does postpone revenue recognition while the associated infrastructure continues consuming capital, which becomes particularly important when management still expects approximately $15B in additional fiscal 2027 capital expenditures.

Roughly $9B is supported by cash, committed financing and customer prepayments, leaving another $6B dependent on additional funding, while last quarter's $529M in operating cash flow included $645M from deferred revenue movements against approximately $4.8B in infrastructure and GPU spending.

That is why I actually view management's decision to moderate expansion rather than pursue growth at any cost favorably, because the next phase of IREN's transformation needs to be about converting contracted capacity into recurring earnings while reducing its dependence on increasingly expensive external capital.

Ultimately, this is why I believe IREN could be one of the most mispriced opportunities in AI infrastructure heading into 2027, particularly when its valuation has compressed substantially relative to competitors like $NBIS despite strengthening customer economics, expanding contracted demand and ownership of increasingly scarce physical infrastructure.

At valuations below two times management's targeted $4B operating ARR, I find the potential risk/reward increasingly compelling, although that target is not yet recognized annual revenue and the company's substantial debt and potential dilution need to be considered before calling the stock inexpensive.

What gives me conviction is that 2027 should finally provide the operating evidence investors have been waiting for, as the remaining Microsoft deployments enter service, additional contracts begin generating revenue and the market gets a clearer picture of the economic returns IREN can produce from its infrastructure investments.

The most important milestones for me will be reaching the operational ARR target without further material delays, securing the remaining financing on attractive terms and demonstrating that revenue per deployed megawatt can translate into sustainable cash generation after depreciation, interest expense and ongoing capital requirements.

If management delivers on those objectives without excessive shareholder dilution, I think investors could eventually recognize that IREN is becoming a vertically integrated AI infrastructure company with scarce power assets, increasingly predictable revenue and substantial operating leverage.

And that's ultimately where my conviction comes from because I believe 2027 could be the year the market finally stops valuing IREN based on how much capital it needs to spend and starts valuing it based on the economic returns that capital is beginning to generate.

➤ 10 tasks in four groups of skills: embodied reasoning, pick and place, assembly, tool use, and mobility

➤ For each task, a model first plays five practice episodes to learn the environment and take notes. It’s then evaluated on ten new scenes

➤ Every evaluation scene changes the room, the lighting, the layout, the props, and the details of the task

➤ Each episode is scored 0 to 100 from the simulator's measurements, with partial credit

No, I do not believe that we should “surrender human free will” to AI systems, and it’s absurd to suggest that I do. I have written hundreds of pages of essays and a constant theme in them is the need for AI to be governed by legitimate democratic processes. For millennia (going all the way back to Greek and Roman philosophers), advocates of autocracy have claimed that it leads to better, faster, or more decisive decision-making than the messy process of democracy. Even if this were true (which I doubt!), we should never sacrifice legitimacy or self-determination at the altar of efficiency or security. This argument against autocracy applies word for word against governance by AI, and I feel equally strongly that turning over governance to AI is a bad idea.

No one who had carefully read my writing or my interviews could reasonably conclude that I believe anything different. For example in an interview on CBS a couple months ago, I specifically called for AI to be governed democratically. I call for the same in Policy on the AI Exponential, Machines of Loving Grace, and The Adolescence of Technology, and We Must Pace the Frontier. Machines of Loving Grace contains an extended section on using AI to revitalize democracy, and discusses the use of AI as an aid to citizens in their decision-making, "aggregat[ing] opinions and driv[ing] consensus among citizens, resolving conflict, finding common ground, and seeking compromise.” The clear and obvious implication is that humans should remain the ones making political and governance decisions. The Adolescence of Technology has an entire section on fighting against AI-driven tyranny, and I even discuss the danger of AI labs usurping power and come out strongly against it — by implication, this definitely includes an AI lab usurping power and giving it to AI itself!

If I thought any of this was a good idea, I would be advocating for it in public, just as I have not been afraid to advocate for many, many unpopular views over the last few years. But I am not advocating for it, because I think turning over governance to AI is a terrible idea.

Separately, I think there is frequent conflation (including in this article) between the idea of “surrendering human free will” to AI in some grand sense of global governance, and the more prosaic idea that as AI systems advance, they become capable of doing specific tasks in a more automated way. This is not AI “running the world,” but AI driving a car, designing a cancer drug, or writing software end-to-end. Here, my view is mixed. AI doing more complete or larger tasks is economically valuable and can drive important advances in software, medicine, transportation, energy, etc. It is clearly desirable in many cases and will save a lot of lives. But it has downsides as well, and in some areas it may not be worth it.

For example, using AI too autonomously to build the next generation of AI systems (known as recursive self-improvement, or RSI) may cause AI to improve faster than we can control or adjust to it, so we may want limits on this process. As we said publicly in early November, we don’t expect it to be safe for Claude to build successive frontier models fully autonomously, without meaningful human supervision or understanding. Second, in some contexts, using AI in too end-to-end a manner may be a cause of serious job disruption, and it may make sense to slow or even stop some AI deployments to give people more time to adapt. Third, while the use of AI for alignment research is an incredibly valuable tool, it must be done with caution, because we may not be able to trust the work of the AI system. Finally, in many cases, humans would simply prefer to do some activities themselves, so they can stay deeply engaged in what matters to them, even if AI can do those activities better. item.title: @mingchikuo：分析指出仅凭电力供应和TDP评估AI晶片出货量过于简化且忽视实际运作
item.description:
AI chip (GPU / TPU) shipments are limited by several factors. But estimating shipment volume from just infrastructure power supply and max chip power (TDP) oversimplifies things and ignores how it actually works in practice. Here's why:

1. Chips don't run at max power all the time.
2. Same power, newer chips produce more tokens. That drives demand for new chips.
3. Same power, more chips running in parallel at lower load will often produce more tokens than fewer chips at high or full load.

item.description:

1. 晶片不會一直以最大功耗運轉。
